row.note: The commentary warns against driving a camel beyond its capacity; Exodus says to help an enemy's donkey when it collapses under its load. The law makes relief of the working animal a duty even toward an enemy.
The source's care for the mount has a concrete legal counterpart: do not look away when a brother's donkey or ox has fallen; help raise it.
The commentary presents the camel as a worker; the law forbids muzzling an ox while it threshes, joining animal labor to its right to eat.
The commentary glosses aslahtu as treating the animal well; Proverbs says a righteous person knows the needs of a beast, while the wicked person's compassion is cruel.

row.basis: donkey beaten for leaving the road
row.note: Balaam strikes his donkey when it turns off the road to avoid the angel; the animal that seems to stumble is responding to danger its rider cannot see.
The source distinguishes the human rider from the animal he rides; Balaam's donkey speaks to protest repeated blows, giving the working animal a voice.
The angel asks why Balaam beat his donkey and says Balaam's way is perverse; the rider's treatment, rather than the animal's refusal, is judged.
The donkey's turns preserve Balaam's life, and the angel says it would otherwise have killed him. This reverses the assumption that the mount is merely a burden-bearing tool.
Abraham saddles a donkey and prepares wood for the journey to Moriah; the animal carries the party's travel burden toward a mountain.
Isaac carries the wood for the offering as father and son climb; beside the source's loaded camel and mountain road, the human traveler also bears a physical load.
The servant takes ten camels and Abraham's goods on a long journey; this is a specific caravan scene joining camel, human travel, and carried property.
Rebekah draws water until the camels finish drinking; beside the commentary's reliable mount and care for an animal, hospitality includes the beasts' needs.
Rebekah and her attendants mount camels and follow Abraham's servant to Isaac, a close scene of human travel on the animal the commentary describes.
The oracle pictures Judah's envoys carrying wealth on young donkeys and camels through a dangerous land. It joins loaded beasts to a journey whose destination is trouble.
Unlike the commentary's mount carrying a traveler, Bel and Nebo are cargo on beasts' backs; the idols themselves stoop as their carriers tire.
The idols cannot rescue their load or themselves from captivity; Isaiah reverses the image of a dependable carrier by making the supposed gods helpless burdens.
The commentary says the human took up the trust; Isaiah's God says Israel has been carried from the womb, shifting the bearer from human to God.
God promises to carry Israel through old age and gray hairs; this gives the load image a sustaining, lifelong meaning rather than an exhausting one.

row.basis: God carries Israel like a parent
row.note: The wilderness journey is remembered as God carrying Israel as a man carries his son; the verse directly joins human travel, a bearer, and a carried person.
God describes bringing Israel out of Egypt as carrying them on eagles' wings; this makes the animal-carrier image an expression of rescue.
The shepherd gathers lambs and carries them in his bosom while gently leading nursing ewes; the source's animal-care gloss meets an image of carrying that protects the vulnerable.
God says he taught Ephraim to walk and took them by the arms; this reverses the source's human rider and animal's working legs into a caregiver supporting a dependent.
God leads with cords of kindness, lifts the yoke from Israel's jaws, and bends to feed them; the image directly answers the source's warning against overdriving a beast.
The psalm says God bears his people day by day; the commentary's human-borne trust is reframed as a load God carries for humans.
The speaker says his iniquities are a burden too heavy for him; this makes the source's load-bearing image explicitly moral and beyond-capacity.

The prophet pictures God weighed down like a cart full of sheaves to announce judgment; this is a concrete image of a load beyond ordinary capacity, though the speaker and moral force differ from the commentary.
The servant bears others' sicknesses and carries their pains; this gives the commentary's burden image a different bearer, one who takes others' suffering upon himself.
The commentary's ṣabīr is glossed as a mountain; the psalm says God gives the speaker deer-like feet and sets him securely on heights, joining sure footing, animal movement, and ascent.
The prophet lists failed fruit trees and empty stalls, a concrete material loss; this gives the surah's opening claim of loss an agricultural scene before the response in the next verses.
Despite the failed harvest and absent herd, the speaker rejoices in YHWH; this supplies a specific response to loss unlike a simple accounting of what remains.
After naming loss, the prophet says God gives feet like a deer's to tread on high places; the verse joins endurance through deprivation to the source's steep mountain path.

God challenges Jeremiah: if footmen have wearied him, how will he contend with horses? The image tests a traveler's endurance as conditions become harder, matching the commentary's concern with capacity.
The poem asks who released the wild donkey, which scorns the city and its driver; beside the source's trained work camel, it presents an animal outside human control.
The wild donkey searches the mountains for pasture rather than following a human road; this gives the source's animal-and-mountain pairing a different, free animal's route.
God asks who gives the horse its might; beside the commentary's emaciated horse driven too hard, Job locates strength in the creature's given power.
The psalm pairs the strength of a horse with the legs of a man, the very human-animal labor relation developed by the commentary.
The next verse says God's delight is in those who fear and hope in him, not in horse strength or human legs; it redirects the source's image of a reliable mount toward trust in God.
The psalm contrasts those who rely on chariots and horses with those who invoke YHWH; it questions making the animal mount the object of confidence.
The psalm says YHWH knows the way of the righteous while the way of the wicked perishes; this makes the commentary's road and final loss an explicit ethical route with an outcome.

row.basis: consider the path of your feet
row.note: The proverb tells the hearer to make the path of the feet level and keep the way steady; it connects the commentary's road to deliberate, careful conduct.
The prophet describes a raised highway on which the redeemed walk; this turns the source's opened, well-traveled road into a route marked by holiness and return.
The covenant sets life and death before Israel and commands them to choose life; beside the commentary's claim that outcomes depend on how one carries the load, walking has a consequential choice.
The proverb says an empty manger is clean without oxen, but abundant crops come through the ox's strength; it names the cost and yield of animal labor.

row.basis: ء م ن ↔ אמנ; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's source gloss emûn is a camel secure against tiring or stumbling; the verse calls Moses' supported hands steady (emunah) through battle until sunset. The root table offers only a sound candidate, with steadiness as the contextual bridge.
Moses' hands grow heavy, and Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset; the source's carried load meets a scene where shared support sustains endurance.

row.basis: ء م ن ↔ אמנ; table sound correspondence
row.note: The Arabic source label āmanū means belief; Genesis uses the Hebrew root אמנ when Abram trusts YHWH, and that trust is counted as righteousness. The root link is a candidate, and the verse specifies trust's object and result.

row.basis: ء م ن ↔ אמנ; table sound correspondence
row.note: The source's emûn gloss describes a dependable camel; Deuteronomy calls God faithful and says his work and ways are just, carrying reliability from the animal image to divine character.

row.basis: ء م ن ↔ אמנ; table sound correspondence
row.note: The source's iman is paired with deeds; Habakkuk says the righteous live by faithfulness, in a vision whose fulfillment must be awaited. The shared-root candidate links trust to endurance.
The psalm directly joins trusting YHWH with doing good and dwelling in the land; this is a close ethical formula for the commentary's pairing of belief and righteous deeds.

row.basis: ء م ن ↔ Aramaic אמנ; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's emûn is a reliable camel; Daniel is found faithful in his royal service. The table marks the Aramaic root as a sound candidate, and the context supplies the specific reliability sense.

row.basis: ء ن س ↔ אנש; table notes BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary labels al-insān with Arabic root ء ن س; WLC's enosh belongs to אנש, whose table entry says BDB cites an Arabic cognate. The psalm asks why mortal humanity receives God's care; the next verse's animal dominion is noted separately.
The psalm gives humanity rule over sheep, oxen, and other creatures; beside the commentary's human mounted on a working animal, it frames the relation as human stewardship and dominion.

row.basis: ع م ل ↔ עמל; table sound correspondence
row.note: The source glosses ya'mele as a camel made for work and calls the animal's legs workers; Jacob names the toil of his hands after tending Laban's flocks. The table's root link joins work-beast and human labor.

row.basis: ع م ل ↔ עמל; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's work glosses meet Hebrew עמל, toil: Ecclesiastes asks what gain a person has from all toil under the sun, tying labor to the question of loss.

row.basis: ص ل ح ↔ צלח; table sound correspondence
row.note: The source's ṣalaḥ gloss is treating the animal well; Joshua uses the corresponding Hebrew root for making one's way prosper through keeping the Torah. The shared root and path are specific, though the source's care sense differs.

row.basis: ص ل ح ↔ צלח; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary glosses aslahtu as treating a beast well; beside camels on a marriage journey, the servant wonders whether YHWH has made his journey prosper. This is a cautious root-and-scene link, not a claim that both words mean the same thing.
The commentary calls attention to the human as traveler and bearer; the psalm says God returns mortal humanity to dust, giving that journey a finite endpoint and a mortality sense.
Isaiah imagines valleys lifted and mountains made low so a highway is level; beside the commentary's steep mountain path, the prophetic route is made passable by divine action.
The eagle spreads wings, takes its young, and bears them; this is a specific animal-carrier image of protection, unlike the commentary's working mount.
Jacob sets his children and wives on camels to flee; the verse joins the human family and camel travel, though its story is flight rather than ordinary work.
Ziba brings saddled donkeys loaded with food for David's household in the wilderness; the animals carry supplies that sustain exhausted travelers.
The wall's ruin is so obstructive that Nehemiah's animal cannot pass beneath him; this gives the road-and-mount image a concrete blocked route.
Elijah eats the food provided and travels forty days and nights to Horeb; this is a sustained human journey to a mountain, with nourishment enabling endurance.
The pilgrim song says God will not let the traveler's foot slip; beside the commentary's stony mountain road, it makes secure footing a divine protection.
The psalm says God repays each person according to their work; this gives the commentary's claim that outcomes depend on how the load is carried a specific scriptural formulation.
The nations bring Israel's exiles back to Jerusalem on camels and other mounts; the verse turns caravan travel into a restoration procession.
The psalm warns the hearer not to be like a horse or mule needing bit and bridle; beside the commentary's attentive human-animal relation, it makes control of the mount a moral metaphor.

The law forbids plowing with an ox and donkey yoked together. Read beside the commentary's warning about carrying beyond capacity, it raises the regulation of animal work; the verse itself gives no reason for the pairing rule.
Job asks what a mortal is that God magnifies and tests him; this is a specific counterpoint to the commentary's human traveler whose fate depends on what he bears.

Sirach pairs fodder, stick, and burden for a donkey with bread, discipline, and work for a servant; it directly compares animal load and human labor, while its social hierarchy differs from the commentary's shared moral image.
Sirach tells the learner to put the neck under wisdom's yoke; unlike an animal overloaded by a driver, this is a chosen discipline that becomes fruitful.
Wisdom says the perishable body weighs down the soul; this gives the source's human burden metaphor an inward, bodily meaning.

The rabbinic discussion of unloading and loading reads the biblical commands through the animal's suffering and the duty to relieve it; this sharpens the commentary's limit against overdriving a beast.
The Mishnah contrasts accepting Torah's yoke with bearing the yoke of worldly rule and labor; this makes a human's moral load a chosen discipline, not merely physical weight.
Ezra describes one narrow, dangerous path between fire and water leading to a city and inheritance; it makes hardship on the way a condition of reaching the destination.
A man traveling down from Jerusalem to Jericho is attacked and left half dead; this supplies a concrete road scene in which a human traveler becomes vulnerable.

row.basis: wounded man carried on a beast
row.note: The Samaritan binds the man's wounds and puts him on his own animal; the beast carries a human who cannot continue under his own strength.
The Samaritan leaves money and instructs the innkeeper to care for the wounded traveler; the aid begun on the road continues as practical responsibility.
Jesus says people untie an ox or donkey on the Sabbath to lead it to water; this directly treats animal care as a legitimate obligation.

row.basis: rescue an ox from a well
row.note: Jesus asks who would not immediately pull a son or ox from a well even on Sabbath; the animal's danger makes rescue more urgent than ritual restriction.
Paul quotes the command not to muzzle an ox threshing grain; the commentary's work-camel and working legs meet a text that protects an animal doing labor.
Paul applies the threshing image to those who plow and thresh in hope of sharing the harvest; the verse explicitly moves from animal work to human labor.
Jesus compares a camel passing through a needle's eye with a rich person entering God's kingdom; the image reverses the camel's ordinary capacity to carry loads and travel.
Jesus contrasts the broad way leading to destruction with an entrance many choose; this joins the commentary's road image to a moral outcome.
The narrow gate and constricted way lead to life and are found by few; this resembles the commentary's steep route and the effort required to reach its outcome.
Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come for rest; this gives the commentary's human load an answer in relief rather than further exertion.
Jesus asks disciples to take his yoke and learn from him, promising rest; the yoke is a chosen teaching relation rather than an overloaded animal's burden.
Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light, a direct contrast to the commentary's camel driven beyond its strength.
Jesus says scribes and Pharisees bind heavy burdens on others' shoulders but will not move them with a finger; the image indicts the human driver who imposes loads without helping.
Paul says God will not let testing exceed what people can bear and provides a way through it; this extends the commentary's concern with overloading from an animal to moral endurance.
Paul commands believers to carry one another's burdens; it turns load-bearing into mutual care, close to the source's mutual urging toward truth and patience.
Paul also says each person will carry their own load; beside 6:2, it distinguishes personal responsibility from burdens shared with others.
Paul describes eternal life for those who persist in doing good; this joins the commentary's righteous deeds with its patience and outcome.
Paul says affliction produces endurance; it gives the commentary's ṣabr on the stony ascent a specific process rather than a static virtue.
The letter remembers the work produced by faith and the steadfastness of hope; this closely joins the commentary's belief, deeds, and patience.
The audience is told to lay aside every weight and run with endurance; this combines the commentary's load, path, and patience in an athletic image.
The verse defines the saints by endurance, keeping God's commandments, and faith in Jesus; it brings together the commentary's patience, good action, and belief.
Jesus calls himself the way and the truth; this is a specific meeting of the commentary's road image with its developed ḥaqq/truth image, though John's claim is about access to the Father.
The Son of Man repays each according to what they have done; this supplies a concrete outcome-for-action formula beside the commentary's claim that how the load is carried determines the result.
Ephesians says salvation is God's gift through faith and not from oneself; this differs in emphasis from the surah's joined condition of belief and righteous deeds.
Ephesians explicitly excludes works as the basis for boasting; the contrast is about the ground of salvation, not a claim that the letter rejects ethical action.
The next verse says believers are created in Christ for good works prepared for them; it reconnects faith and action while making works the result of grace.
James says faith without works is dead; this closely matches the commentary's pairing of belief with righteous deeds.
James says Abraham's faith was active together with his works and completed by them; belief and action are mutually expressed rather than separated.

row.basis: justified by works and not faith alone
row.note: James explicitly says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone; beside the surah's joined faith-and-deed formula, this shows a Christian argument over how the two relate.
The audience needs endurance after doing God's will to receive what is promised; this joins action, patience, and final outcome.
Jesus tells followers to deny themselves, take up their cross daily, and follow him; this makes a carried burden part of a sustained path of discipleship.
Sirach says the farmer's wisdom is in his fieldwork and labor; this gives the commentary's working animal and human labor a specific agricultural setting.
The Sabbath command gives the ox and donkey rest and allows the servant to be refreshed; this adds a recurring limit on animal labor to the commentary's warning about overdriving a mount.

row.basis: know the state of the flock
row.note: The proverb tells the keeper to know the condition of his flock and attend to the herds; this makes the commentary's dependable animal and good treatment an ongoing duty of attention.
God asks whether the wild ox will serve or stay by a manger; beside the commentary's camel trained for work, Job distinguishes a creature's nature from its use as a work animal.
The poem asks whether a human can bind the wild ox to a furrow; this tests whether strength and labor can simply be imposed on an animal.
God asks whether Job would rely on the wild ox's great strength; the question specifically joins trust to an animal's carrying and working capacity.
The poem asks whether the wild ox will bring the harvest into the barn; it contrasts a trained worker such as the source's ya'mele with a strong animal that cannot be assumed to serve human labor.
Those who wait for YHWH renew their strength, mount up with wings, run without weariness, and walk without fainting; this directly joins trust, animal-like movement, and endurance on the road.

The source glosses emûn as a dependable camel; God calls Moses faithful in the divine household. The Hebrew אמנ root is the table's sound-correspondence candidate, and this verse gives the human stewardship sense.

row.basis: ع م ل ↔ עמל; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's source labels from ع م ل describe work and labor; Isaiah says the servant sees the toil of his soul and is satisfied, then bears others' iniquities. This joins labor, burden, and its outcome through the table's candidate root.

row.basis: ء ن س ↔ Aramaic אנש; table sound correspondence
row.note: The source labels al-insān with Arabic ء ن س; Daniel's Aramaic figure is “like a son of man,” appearing after the beastly kingdoms. The table marks אנש as a sound candidate, and the scene makes human likeness distinct from beasts.
The next verse gives the human-like figure dominion over peoples and nations; beside the commentary's rider among working beasts, this extends the human-animal contrast into a vision of rule.
The psalm says young lions roar for prey and seek their food from God; the animal has its own work and dependence within the created order, alongside the human labor named in verse 23.
At sunrise the lions withdraw to their dens; the next verse sends humans out to work. This day-night ordering gives the commentary's human and animal labor a distinct shared setting.
The psalm says a human goes out to work until evening, after describing animals' night activity; this places human toil and animal life in one daily rhythm.
The proverb commands trust in YHWH rather than reliance on one's own understanding; this makes the commentary's iman-as-reliability image a relation of dependence, not merely confidence in a mount.
The proverb says to acknowledge God in all one's ways and he will make the paths straight; it joins trust to the road image developed by the commentary.

The Shunammite orders her servant not to slow the donkey while she rushes to Elisha; the commentary warns about driving an animal beyond capacity. The text records urgency but does not say the donkey is harmed, so the contrast is limited.
Sirach continues its yoke image by saying wisdom's fetters become protection and her collar a glorious robe; this clarifies that its burden is chosen discipline, unlike the source's overworked beast.
The saying that the work is not yours to finish, yet you are not free to desist, gives labor a patience dimension close to the commentary's joining of work and ṣabr.

The Rule of the Community contrasts the ways and lots of truth and perversity and their final outcomes; it offers a Jewish ethical map of conduct and consequence beside the commentary's human path from loss to right action.
James says the testing of faith produces endurance; this gives the commentary's ṣabr a process rooted in belief rather than mere physical toughness.
James says endurance must complete its work so the hearer becomes mature and whole; this joins patience, action, and a result.
Paul continues that endurance produces tested character and hope; it extends the commentary's mountain-road patience into a sequence with an outcome.
The prayer asks that believers bear fruit in every good work; this directly resonates with the commentary's righteous deeds and its image of a productive worker.
The next verse asks for strength to endure and be patient; it explicitly joins good work with the source's ṣabr.
The message to Ephesus names its works, toil, and patient endurance; it brings together the commentary's labor and persistence in one concrete community assessment.
The Ephesians have endured and not grown weary; the wording adds the specific question of fatigue developed in the commentary's reliable, untiring mount.
The message to Thyatira lists works, love, faith, service, and patient endurance, and says the later works exceed the first; this is a close formula joining belief, action, and perseverance.

row.basis: labor in the Lord is not vain
row.note: Paul urges steadfastness and abundant work because labor in the Lord is not in vain; this answers the surah's loss language with a specific claim about enduring work.
Paul tells believers not to grow weary in doing good, since they will reap if they do not give up; this closely joins righteous action, endurance, and outcome.
The letter tells the community not to grow weary in doing good; it adds a direct communal exhortation to the commentary's mutual counsel toward patience.
God is not unjust to forget the readers' work and the love they showed in serving the saints; this connects labor to care for others and to divine remembrance.

row.basis: inherit promises through faith and patience
row.note: The audience is told to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience; this explicitly joins belief, endurance, and final outcome.
Paul says the affliction in Asia burdened the group beyond their strength and brought despair of life; this is a direct human counterpart to the commentary's load beyond capacity.
Paul says the experience taught them not to rely on themselves but on God who raises the dead; this continues the beyond-capacity burden with a specific turn toward trust.
Peter tells readers to cast their anxieties on God because he cares for them; this turns the human burden into a load entrusted to a caring bearer.
Peter says Christ bore sins in his body on the tree; this gives the load image a specific moral sense and a bearer who carries others' wrongdoing.
Paul says the strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak rather than please themselves; this makes carrying a communal duty of care, not only an individual's burden.
Four people bring a paralytic to Jesus by carrying him; this is a concrete scene of humans bearing another person's weight so he can reach help.

row.basis: love as the weight that carries
row.note: Augustine calls love a person's weight, the force that carries one toward one's destination; this Christian interpretation turns the commentary's physical load and road into an account of moral desire.
